description: We are a team of data science and analytics enthusiasts tackling the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge. Our goal is to leverage NASA satellite data, exploratory data analysis, and predictive modeling in Python to identify, quantify, and visualize key environmental trends and anomalies.
summary:
We built EarthSignal to help people explore climate trends and understand how much confidence to place in them. Users can choose two locations around the world and compare temperature or rainfall using NASA POWER data. The app shows annual charts, trends per decade and statistical uncertainty, with options to download the data and results.

Our Karachi case study uses 288 monthly temperature observations from NASA Giovanni’s MERRA-2 dataset, covering 2001–2024. We found a small upward trend of about 0.069°C per decade, but the evidence was not strong enough to call it statistically significant. Showing that uncertainty honestly is an important part of our project.

EarthSignal addresses “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” by making NASA climate data easier to explore and question. It explains where the data comes from, how trends are calculated and what the results can—and cannot—tell us. We designed it for students, educators and anyone curious about changes in Earth’s climate.
details:
We built EarthSignal around a simple question: when a climate chart goes up or down, how do we know whether it shows a clear trend or just year-to-year variation?

Our project gives users a way to explore that question with NASA data. It combines a global comparison tool with a documented regional investigation of Karachi.

How it works

In the Explorer, users choose two locations, select temperature or precipitation, and set a time period. EarthSignal retrieves monthly records from NASA POWER and turns them into annual values. Temperature averages account for the number of days in each month, while precipitation is converted into annual totals. Incomplete years are excluded.

The results include annual charts, a trend per decade, a 95% confidence interval and a p-value. Users can download the annual data and an investigation summary to review or use in their own work.

Our Karachi investigation

We also examined 288 monthly temperature observations from NASA Giovanni’s MERRA-2 dataset for 2001–2024. This case study uses a regional average, which is different from the grid-cell data used in the Explorer.

The estimated temperature trend was approximately +0.069°C per decade, with a p-value of 0.442 and a 95% confidence interval from about −0.114 to +0.253°C per decade. Under the statistical assumptions used, this result is inconclusive. It does not establish significant warming, but it also does not prove that no change occurred.

What makes EarthSignal useful

We wanted uncertainty to be part of the main experience. EarthSignal explains the source of its data, the calculations behind each trend and the limits of the conclusions. A weak or inconclusive result is still worth showing: it helps users ask better questions instead of treating every upward line as proof.

We designed the project for students, educators and curious users. It could support classroom investigations and comparisons between places, although we have not yet measured its educational impact.

Tools and limitations

We built the web app with React, TypeScript and TanStack Start, using Recharts for charts and Tailwind CSS for styling. Lovable and ChatGPT assisted with development, writing and review. The illustrative Earth artwork is AI-generated and labelled accordingly; it is not NASA observational imagery.

Trends are calculated using ordinary least squares regression. The reported intervals and p-values use classical assumptions and do not adjust for serial correlation or multiple comparisons. NASA’s gridded records also do not represent individual weather stations. Comparing two trend estimates does not by itself establish that their difference is statistically significant, and the app does not identify the causes of any observed change.
